name: C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema types I and II)

reference.source: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice / WAO-EAACI hereditary angioedema guidance
clinicalPearls: Causes recurrent non-pruritic, non-urticarial angio-oedema of the skin, gastrointestinal tract and upper airway, with attacks that are bradykinin-mediated
Type I (about 85 percent) has low antigenic and functional C1 inhibitor; type II has normal or high antigenic level but reduced C1-inhibitor function
A persistently low complement C4 is a useful screening clue between and during attacks
Attacks lack the wheals of histaminergic angio-oedema and characteristically do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline
Laryngeal oedema can be fatal, and unexplained abdominal attacks may mimic a surgical abdomen
Attacks are triggered by trauma, dental or surgical procedures, infection, oestrogens and ACE inhibitors

Management separates on-demand attack treatment, short-term procedural prophylaxis, and long-term prophylaxis using C1-inhibitor concentrate or bradykinin-pathway-directed agents rather than antihistamines/steroids
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by SERPING1 mutations that reduce the quantity (type I) or function (type II) of C1 inhibitor. C1 inhibitor is the principal brake on the contact (kallikrein-kinin) system as well as on the classical complement and fibrinolytic pathways. When it is deficient, unrestrained activation of plasma kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to release bradykinin, a potent vasodilator that increases vascular permeability. The resulting fluid extravasation produces the localised, self-limiting but potentially life-threatening swelling, and the mechanism explains why the swelling is bradykinin-driven rather than histamine-driven and does not respond to antiallergic therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Histaminergic (mast-cell/allergic) angio-oedema with or without urticaria
Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency associated with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease
Hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor (e.g. factor XII or plasminogen mutations)
Gastrointestinal or surgical causes of recurrent abdominal pain
additionalInvestigations: Complement C4 level as an initial screen
C1-inhibitor functional assay to distinguish type II
C1q level to help separate hereditary from acquired deficiency
SERPING1 genetic testing when biochemistry is equivocal or for family studies
Investigation for underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease if acquired deficiency is suspected
redFlags: Laryngeal or tongue swelling with any voice change, stridor or difficulty swallowing
Rapidly progressive facial or neck oedema threatening the airway
Severe unexplained abdominal attacks that could be mistaken for an acute surgical abdomen
Attacks provoked or worsened by an ACE inhibitor or oestrogen therapy
reference.prognosis: With accurate diagnosis and access to modern on-demand and prophylactic therapy the outlook is good and quality of life can be near normal, but untreated laryngeal attacks carry a real risk of asphyxiation, making airway attacks the principal cause of mortality.
pitfalls: Treating bradykinin-mediated attacks as allergic and relying on antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline, which do not work for hereditary angioedema attacks
Being falsely reassured by a normal C1-inhibitor antigenic level in type II, where function is the abnormal parameter
Continuing ACE inhibitors or oestrogen-containing therapy that provoke attacks
Overlooking short-term prophylaxis before dental or surgical procedures
references: WAO-EAACI Guideline for the Management of Hereditary Angioedema
